title: Clinical and molecular prognostic factors associated with outcomes of first-line osimertinib in EGFR-Mutated advanced NSCLC: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
abstract: Background.
Osimertinib is the standard first-line therapy for epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR)-mutated advanced non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), but outcomes remain heterogeneous.
This meta-analysis evaluated baseline clinical and molecular prognostic factors associated with poorer outcomes in this setting.
Methods.
PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, Scopus, and the Cochrane Library were searched through 20 May 2026.
Eligible studies included patients with EGFR-mutated advanced, recurrent, or metastatic NSCLC receiving first-line osimertinib with extractable prognostic data.
The primary outcome was progression-free survival or real-world progression-free survival (PFS/rwPFS); overall survival or real-world overall survival (OS/rwOS) was secondary.
Hazard ratios (HRs) were pooled using random-effects models.
Results.
Eighteen studies involving 4,070 first-line osimertinib-treated patients were included.
TP53 mutation was associated with shorter PFS/rwPFS (HR 1.65, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.15-2.37) and worse OS/rwOS (HR 1.55, 95% CI 1.14-2.12).

EGFR L858R, versus exon 19 deletion, was associated with shorter PFS/rwPFS (HR 1.62, 95% CI 1.39-1.90) and worse OS/rwOS (HR 1.63, 95% CI 1.40-1.88), with consistent estimates across sensitivity analyses.
Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status ≥ 2, central nervous system/brain metastasis, and liver metastasis were associated with poorer outcomes.
The OS/rwOS association for liver metastasis was sensitive to alternative estimate selection.
Evidence for bone metastasis and programmed death-ligand 1 expression was less robust.
Conclusions.
Evidence-tier assessment identified EGFR L858R, ECOG PS ≥ 2, and CNS/brain metastasis as high-certainty adverse prognostic factors.
Liver metastasis was supported by moderate certainty for PFS/rwPFS but lower certainty for OS/rwOS.
TP53 mutation, PD-L1 expression, and bone metastasis were lower-certainty or exploratory findings.
These findings support future integrated prognostic models, but do not establish criteria for selecting intensified first-line therapy over osimertinib monotherapy.

body.text: EGFR-mutated advanced non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) illustrates a central tension in precision oncology: a targetable driver can guide treatment selection, but it does not fully define prognosis.
Lung cancer accounted for nearly 2.5 million new cases and 1.8 million deaths worldwide in 2022 [].
In metastatic oncogene-addicted NSCLC, treatment selection now integrates driver mutation status with metastatic distribution, performance status, and clinically relevant co-alterations [].
However, patients with EGFR-mutated advanced NSCLC still experience divergent outcomes despite receiving the same molecularly matched first-line therapy.
Precision at the level of EGFR mutation is therefore necessary, but it is not sufficient for individualized risk assessment.
Osimertinib, a third-generation EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI), is the preferred first-line therapy for EGFR-mutated advanced NSCLC.
FLAURA established its superiority over first-generation EGFR-TKIs, and the final survival analysis confirmed an overall survival advantage [, ].
Its central nervous system activity further strengthened its role, particularly for patients with baseline brain or central nervous system involvement [].
Nevertheless, outcomes under first-line osimertinib vary substantially.
Some patients achieve prolonged disease control, whereas others progress early despite apparently appropriate molecular selection.
This heterogeneity has become more clinically important as first-line strategies move beyond osimertinib monotherapy.

FLAURA2 showed that adding platinum-pemetrexed chemotherapy to osimertinib improved progression-free survival, and the subsequent survival analysis suggested an overall survival advantage for the combination strategy [, ].
MARIPOSA also showed longer progression-free survival with amivantamab plus lazertinib than with osimertinib in previously untreated EGFR-mutated advanced NSCLC [].
These regimens expand treatment options, but they also create a practical risk-benefit dilemma.
More intensive first-line therapy may improve disease control in selected patients, but it can also increase toxicity, treatment burden, and cost.
A clinically useful risk-stratification framework is therefore needed as a foundation for future risk-adapted studies.
However, prognostic evidence from osimertinib-treated cohorts cannot by itself determine which patients should receive osimertinib monotherapy or intensified first-line therapy.
Treatment heterogeneity is multifactorial.
Acquired resistance to first-line osimertinib is molecularly diverse, with MET amplification, EGFR C797S, and other alterations observed rather than one dominant resistance mechanism [].
Baseline tumor biology may also influence benefit before acquired resistance emerges.
EGFR exon 19 deletion and exon 21 L858R are both sensitizing mutations, but clinical outcomes may differ between these two subtypes [].

Other molecular markers, including TP53 co-mutation, programmed death-ligand 1 expression, circulating tumor DNA dynamics, and EGFR mutation abundance, have also been linked to less favorable outcomes in some studies [-].

Meanwhile, host vulnerability and aggressive metastatic tropism, reflected by poor performance status, central nervous system involvement, liver or bone metastasis, and higher metastatic burden, may further shape the depth and durability of benefit from osimertinib [, ].
Despite this expanding literature, evidence on prognostic factors after first-line osimertinib remains fragmented and has not yet produced a reproducible definition of baseline high-risk disease.
Individual studies often focus on a single biomarker, one metastatic site, or a selected real-world cohort.
Exposure definitions, biomarker thresholds, endpoint selection, adjustment strategy, and HR reporting also vary substantially.
These differences make it difficult to distinguish robust prognostic factors from findings that are underpowered, inconsistently defined, or insufficiently adjusted.

This systematic review and meta-analysis therefore synthesized available evidence on baseline clinical and molecular prognostic factors associated with poorer outcomes in EGFR-mutated advanced NSCLC treated with first-line osimertinib.

First-line osimertinib was treated as the common treatment background; baseline clinical or molecular factors were evaluated as exposures; and lower-risk or absent-feature groups served as comparators.

The aim was not to reassess osimertinib efficacy or to determine which patients derive greater benefit from treatment intensification, but to clarify which pretreatment characteristics are associated with poorer outcomes within a common first-line osimertinib treatment background.

This systematic review and meta-analysis was conducted in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 statement [] and the methodological guidance of the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions [].
The protocol was prospectively registered in the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO; registration number: CRD420261413136).
The review question, eligibility criteria, outcome hierarchy, data extraction strategy, and quantitative synthesis plan were specified before data pooling.
This review focused on baseline clinical and molecular prognostic factors associated with poorer outcomes in patients with EGFR-mutated advanced NSCLC treated with first-line osimertinib.
Because this was a prognostic-factor meta-analysis, osimertinib was considered the common treatment background.
The exposures of interest were prognostic factors measured before or at the start of first-line osimertinib rather than therapeutic interventions.
This review evaluated prognostic associations within a common first-line osimertinib treatment background and was not designed to assess predictive treatment effects.
Therefore, the identified baseline factors were not interpreted as biomarkers of differential benefit from osimertinib-based combination therapy or other treatment-intensification strategies.
A systematic literature search was performed in PubMed, Embase, Web of Science Core Collection, Scopus, and the Cochrane Library from database inception through 20 May 2026.

The search was designed to identify clinical studies evaluating baseline clinical or molecular prognostic factors associated with outcomes in patients with EGFR-mutated advanced NSCLC treated with first-line osimertinib.
The search date was selected to capture the most recent evidence available before data extraction and analysis were finalized.

The search strategy combined five prespecified concept groups: advanced, metastatic, unresectable, recurrent, or stage IV NSCLC or lung adenocarcinoma terms; EGFR mutation terms; osimertinib terms; first-line or treatment-naive setting terms; and prognostic, predictive, biomarker, or outcome-related terms.
Individual prognostic factors, including TP53 mutation, EGFR L858R, PD-L1 expression, liver metastasis, CNS/brain metastasis, and bone metastasis, were not used as mandatory search terms.
This strategy was intended to avoid missing studies that reported these factors only in the full text, tables, figures, or supplementary materials.
Search strategies were adapted to the syntax of each database.
Reference lists of included studies and relevant reviews were manually screened to identify additional eligible studies.
The complete search strategy is provided in the Supplementary Material.

Studies were considered eligible when they met all of the following criteria: (1) adult patients with unresectable, advanced, recurrent, or metastatic NSCLC harboring activating EGFR mutations; (2) osimertinib evaluated as first-line systemic therapy for advanced or metastatic disease, or separately extractable data for a first-line osimertinib subgroup; (3) at least one baseline clinical or molecular prognostic factor assessed before or at the start of first-line osimertinib; (4) at least one eligible outcome reported, including progression-free survival (PFS), real-world progression-free survival (rwPFS), overall survival (OS), real-world overall survival (rwOS), time to next treatment (TTNT), time to treatment discontinuation (TTD), duration of response (DoR), objective response rate (ORR), or disease control rate (DCR); and (5) extractable comparative data available for the association between at least one prognostic factor and at least one eligible outcome.
Eligible study designs included prospective cohort studies, retrospective cohort studies, real-world studies, registry-based studies, and prognostic or biomarker subgroup analyses of clinical trials.
Only peer-reviewed, full-text original clinical studies published in English were considered eligible.

Studies were excluded when they met any of the following criteria: (1) reviews, systematic reviews, meta-analyses, editorials, comments, protocols, conference abstracts without sufficient data, case reports, animal studies, cell experiments, or basic mechanistic studies; (2) studies focused on early-stage, perioperative, neoadjuvant, adjuvant, or postoperative osimertinib without separately extractable advanced or metastatic first-line osimertinib data; (3) studies evaluating osimertinib as second-line or later-line therapy after acquired EGFR T790M-mediated resistance without separately extractable first-line osimertinib data; (4) studies evaluating mixed EGFR-TKI regimens or mixed treatment lines without separately extractable first-line osimertinib data; (5) studies limited to overall treatment efficacy, mutation prevalence, baseline characteristics, or descriptive biomarker distribution without prognostic factor-outcome association data; (6) studies without extractable comparative data for any eligible prognostic factor-outcome pair; (7) studies with unavailable full text; and (8) non-English publications.
When overlapping patient populations were suspected, the same cohort was not entered more than once in any single pooled analysis.

For overlapping reports, priority was given to the study with the largest sample size, longest follow-up, clearest first-line osimertinib population, most complete prognostic factor data, or most appropriate effect estimate.
Alternative estimates from overlapping reports were reserved for sensitivity analyses when applicable.
Two reviewers independently screened all retrieved records.
After duplicate removal, titles and abstracts were reviewed for potential eligibility.
Full texts of potentially relevant articles were then assessed against the prespecified inclusion and exclusion criteria.
Disagreements were resolved by discussion, with consultation from a third reviewer when consensus could not be reached.
Two reviewers independently extracted data using a standardized extraction form.

Study-level variables included first author, publication year, country or region, study design, data source, study period, number of centers, sample size, tumor type, treatment setting, and follow-up duration.

Patient and disease variables included age, sex, smoking status, histologic subtype, disease stage, ECOG performance status, EGFR mutation subtype, baseline metastatic sites, and previous treatment history when available.
Treatment variables included osimertinib dose, first-line monotherapy or combination treatment, treatment start point, and subsequent therapy when reported.
For each prognostic factor, extracted information included factor definition, assessment method, cutoff value, exposure group, reference group, and number of patients in each group.

Candidate molecular factors included TP53 mutation, EGFR mutation subtype, PD-L1 expression, MET amplification, other gene co-alterations, baseline circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) status, EGFR mutation abundance, and other reported molecular prognostic markers.

Candidate clinical factors included ECOG performance status, liver metastasis, CNS/brain metastasis, bone metastasis, age, sex, smoking status, number of metastatic sites, disease stage, and other baseline characteristics reported by the original studies.
The primary meta-analytic outcome was PFS or rwPFS.

PFS was defined as the time from initiation of first-line osimertinib to disease progression or death, according to the definition used in each original study. rwPFS was extracted when real-world studies used routine clinical assessment, investigator-defined progression, electronic health record-derived progression, or other real-world progression definitions.

The key secondary outcome was OS or rwOS, defined as the time from initiation of first-line osimertinib to death from any cause. rwOS was extracted when survival was reported from real-world data sources.
Other eligible outcomes included TTNT, TTD, DoR, ORR, and DCR when extractable comparative data were available.
ORR was defined as complete response plus partial response, and DCR was defined as complete response, partial response, or stable disease, according to the original study definitions.
For time-to-event outcomes, HRs and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were extracted whenever available.
For dichotomous outcomes, event counts and total numbers were extracted.
Adjusted HRs were prioritized over unadjusted HRs.
When multiple adjusted models were reported, the model with the most clinically relevant covariate adjustment was preferred.
Directly reported HRs were prioritized over HRs estimated from Kaplan-Meier curves or other reconstructed data.
When HRs were not directly reported, they were estimated from Kaplan-Meier curves, log-rank P values, event numbers, or other available statistical information when methodologically appropriate.
Adjustment status and covariates included in multivariable models were recorded.
Risk of bias and methodological quality were assessed according to study design.

For observational cohort studies and real-world studies, methodological quality was evaluated using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS), which assesses selection of study groups, comparability of cohorts, and outcome assessment.
For randomized clinical trials or randomized trial-derived subgroup analyses, risk of bias was assessed using the revised Cochrane risk-of-bias tool for randomized trials (RoB 2).
Because this review focused on prognostic factors, particular attention was given to prognostic-factor measurement, outcome definition, confounder adjustment, and statistical reporting.
Two reviewers independently performed quality assessment, and disagreements were resolved by discussion or consultation with a third reviewer.
Meta-analyses were performed using Review Manager version 5.4.
For time-to-event outcomes, HRs with 95% CIs were pooled using the generic inverse variance method.
HRs were entered as log-transformed HRs with corresponding standard errors.
When standard errors were not directly available, they were derived from reported 95% CIs using standard methods.
For dichotomous outcomes, odds ratios or risk ratios with 95% CIs were planned when event counts were extractable.
Effect directions were standardized so that HR > 1 indicated poorer outcomes in the exposed or high-risk group.
When an original study reported the reverse comparison, the effect estimate was inverted before synthesis.
For response outcomes, event coding was standardized when necessary to keep the direction of effect clinically interpretable across analyses.
Quantitative meta-analysis was performed when at least two studies reported comparable effect estimates for the same prognostic factor and outcome.
When only two studies were available, pooled results were interpreted cautiously and supported by descriptive assessment.
When fewer than two studies reported comparable data, or when definitions were too heterogeneous for pooling, findings were summarized descriptively.

Because PFS and rwPFS, as well as OS and rwOS, differ in assessment schedule, progression ascertainment, and data source, pooled PFS/rwPFS and OS/rwOS estimates were interpreted as clinically related but methodologically heterogeneous time-to-event outcomes rather than strictly trial-defined endpoints.

Separate endpoint-defined syntheses were considered when at least two comparable estimates were available for the same prognostic factor and endpoint definition; otherwise, endpoint heterogeneity was addressed descriptively and in the limitations.
Random-effects models were used for all pooled analyses because clinical and methodological heterogeneity was expected across studies.

Potential sources of heterogeneity included study design, data source, patient population, osimertinib treatment pattern, prognostic-factor definition, molecular testing method, outcome definition, follow-up duration, and adjustment method.
Statistical heterogeneity was assessed using the I2 statistic and Cochran’s Q test.
I2 values greater than 50% were considered to indicate substantial heterogeneity.
Prespecified subgroup analyses were planned when data were sufficient.
These included analyses by study design, data source, EGFR mutation subtype, outcome definition, adjusted versus unadjusted HRs, and tissue-based versus plasma or ctDNA-based molecular testing.

A monotherapy-versus-combination subgroup analysis was also considered; however, after study selection, the assembled evidence base contained no eligible osimertinib-based combination-therapy cohort contributing comparable prognostic HRs.

Therefore, this subgroup analysis could not be performed, and all pooled HRs were interpreted as prognostic associations within a first-line osimertinib treatment background rather than as evidence for treatment selection between monotherapy and combination therapy.
For study-design and data-source analyses, prospective-study-only and non-ELUCIDATOR sensitivity analyses were evaluated for each pooled factor-outcome pair.
Quantitative restricted pooling was performed only when at least two comparable estimates remained after restriction; otherwise, feasibility was reported descriptively in the Supplementary Material.
Sensitivity analyses were performed when alternative data-handling decisions could influence the pooled estimate.

These analyses included exclusion of unadjusted estimates, exclusion of studies with unclear first-line treatment definitions, inclusion or exclusion of studies with non-standard prognostic factor definitions, replacement of overlapping cohorts, inclusion of additional lower-priority estimates, and assessment of directionally inconsistent or imprecise estimates.
Leave-one-out analyses were planned for major pooled outcomes when the number of included studies was sufficient.
To avoid assigning equal interpretive weight to pooled estimates with different evidence depths, each pooled prognostic factor-outcome association was assigned a simple evidence tier.
Tiers were based on the number of contributing studies, consistency of effect direction, statistical heterogeneity, and stability across sensitivity analyses.
High certainty indicated multiple comparable estimates across clinically relevant endpoints with consistent direction and stable sensitivity analyses.
Moderate certainty indicated generally consistent evidence with fewer studies, endpoint-specific support, or some heterogeneity.
Low certainty indicated sparse evidence, inconsistent or sensitivity-dependent results, or lack of a robust association.
These tiers were intended to summarize relative confidence within this review rather than to provide treatment-selection recommendations.
Publication bias was planned to be assessed by funnel plot inspection and Egger’s test when at least 10 studies were included in a single meta-analysis.
When fewer than 10 studies were available, formal publication-bias assessment was not performed because reliability would be low.
A two-sided P value less than 0.05 was considered statistically significant.
The study selection process is presented in Fig. 1.
Eighteen studies met the eligibility criteria and were included in the systematic review [, , -].
Quantitative synthesis was performed according to the availability of extractable prognostic data for each prespecified factor and outcome.
All included studies evaluated patients with EGFR-mutated advanced, metastatic, or recurrent NSCLC treated with first-line osimertinib or with separately extractable first-line osimertinib data.

Prognostic factors included molecular variables, such as TP53 mutation, EGFR mutation subtype, PD-L1 expression, baseline ctDNA status, EGFR mutation abundance, NRG1 alteration, and AXL or p53 protein expression, as well as clinical variables, including ECOG performance status, CNS/brain metastasis, liver metastasis, bone metastasis, age, sex, smoking status, metastatic burden, and disease stage.
The primary meta-analytic outcome was PFS/rwPFS.
OS/rwOS was analyzed as the key secondary outcome.
For time-to-event outcomes, HRs were synthesized using the generic inverse variance method.
Effect direction was standardized so that HR > 1 indicated poorer outcomes in the exposed or high-risk group.
The number of studies included in each meta-analysis differed by prognostic factor and outcome because extractable HRs were not available for every factor-outcome pair.
When overlapping patient populations were suspected, the same cohort was not entered more than once in any single pooled analysis.
The ELUCIDATOR-derived reports were handled conservatively, and alternative estimates from overlapping reports were assessed in sensitivity analyses when applicable [-].
Potential overlap between the two Yoshimura reports was also considered when determining the contribution of PD-L1-related estimates [, ].

Baseline clinicopathologic characteristics are shown in Supplementary Table S1.
Study-level extracted prognostic data are shown in Supplementary Table S2, and the studies contributing to each quantitative synthesis are listed in Supplementary Table S3.
Methodological quality assessment is presented in Table 2.
No included study provided comparable prognostic HRs from an osimertinib-based combination-therapy cohort.
Therefore, the planned monotherapy-versus-combination subgroup analysis was not structurally executable with the assembled evidence base.

To address study-design and data-source heterogeneity, prospective-study-only and non-ELUCIDATOR sensitivity analyses were evaluated across pooled factor-outcome pairs and summarized in Supplementary Table S4.
Quantitative restricted pooling was performed only when at least two comparable estimates remained; otherwise, the analysis was reported as not feasible.

The single RCT-derived post hoc biomarker analysis did not provide a comparable prognostic HR for inclusion in the main pooled estimates, precluding a separate RCT-derived versus observational pooled comparison.
The covariates included in multivariable models contributing adjusted HRs are summarized in Supplementary Table S5.
Two studies were included in the meta-analysis of PFS/rwPFS according to TP53 mutation status [, ].
Using a random-effects model, TP53 mutation was associated with a 65% higher hazard for the PFS/rwPFS endpoint compared with TP53 wild type (HR 1.65, 95% CI 1.15-2.37; P = 0.007; Fig. 2A).
No statistical heterogeneity was observed between the included studies (I2 = 0%; χ2 = 0.03, df = 1, P = 0.86).
For OS/rwOS, three studies were included according to TP53 mutation status [, , ].
TP53 mutation was associated with a 55% higher hazard of death compared with TP53 wild type (HR 1.55, 95% CI 1.14-2.12; P = 0.006; Fig. 2B).
Moderate heterogeneity was observed across the included studies (I2 = 42%; χ2 = 3.45, df = 2, P = 0.18).
Eight studies were included in the main meta-analysis of PFS/rwPFS according to EGFR mutation subtype [, , , , , , , ].
Effect direction was standardized as EGFR L858R versus exon 19 deletion.
EGFR L858R was associated with a 62% higher hazard for the PFS/rwPFS endpoint compared with exon 19 deletion (HR 1.62, 95% CI 1.39-1.90; P < 0.001; Fig. 3A).
No statistical heterogeneity was observed across the included studies (I2 = 0%; χ2 = 3.24, df = 7, P = 0.86).
Sensitivity analyses examined the impact of potentially overlapping cohorts and effect-estimate selection on the PFS/rwPFS analysis.

Replacing the ELUCIDATOR-derived estimate used in the main analysis with the corresponding alternative ELUCIDATOR estimate yielded a comparable pooled effect (HR 1.62, 95% CI 1.38-1.89; P < 0.001; I2 = 0%; Supplementary Fig. S1) [, ].
Additional inclusion of an extractable unadjusted HR for PFS also produced a stable estimate (HR 1.63, 95% CI 1.40-1.90; P < 0.001; I2 = 0%; Supplementary Fig. S2) [].
These findings indicate that the adverse association between EGFR L858R and PFS/rwPFS was consistent across alternative analytical assumptions.
Seven studies were included in the main meta-analysis of OS/rwOS according to EGFR mutation subtype [-, , , ].
EGFR L858R was associated with a 63% higher hazard of death compared with exon 19 deletion (HR 1.63, 95% CI 1.40-1.88; P < 0.001; Fig. 3B).
The estimate was consistent across studies, with no statistical heterogeneity (I2 = 0%; χ2 = 2.95, df = 6, P = 0.81).
A sensitivity analysis addressed the potential overlap between the two ELUCIDATOR reports.

After replacing the ELUCIDATOR-derived estimate used in the main analysis with the alternative ELUCIDATOR estimate, the pooled estimate remained consistent with the main analysis (HR 1.62, 95% CI 1.39-1.88; P < 0.001; I2 = 0%; Supplementary Fig. S3) [, ].
This result indicates that the association between EGFR L858R and poorer OS/rwOS was not materially affected by the selected ELUCIDATOR-derived estimate.
Two studies were included in the main meta-analysis of PFS/rwPFS according to tumor PD-L1 expression [, ].
Effect direction was standardized as PD-L1 high expression versus low or negative expression.
PD-L1 high expression was associated with an 84% higher hazard for the PFS/rwPFS endpoint (HR 1.84, 95% CI 1.15-2.95; P = 0.01; Fig. 4).
No statistical heterogeneity was observed between the included studies (I2 = 0%; χ2 = 0.69, df = 1, P = 0.41).
Sensitivity analyses were conducted because eligible PD-L1 studies used different cutoffs or reported estimates with inconsistent directions.
After inclusion of a study using a PD-L1 TPS cutoff of ≥ 20% rather than ≥ 50%, the pooled association remained significant (HR 1.97, 95% CI 1.31-2.94; P = 0.001; I2 = 0%; Supplementary Fig. S4) [].

By contrast, after inclusion of a study reporting an extractable HR for PD-L1 TPS ≥ 50% but with a point estimate directionally inconsistent with its Kaplan-Meier median PFS pattern and with the other eligible studies, the pooled association was attenuated and no longer statistically significant (HR 1.46, 95% CI 0.77-2.78; P = 0.25; I2 = 50%; Supplementary Fig. S5) [].
Therefore, the main PFS/rwPFS signal for high PD-L1 expression should be interpreted cautiously because it depended on effect-estimate selection.
Only one study reported an eligible effect estimate for OS according to tumor PD-L1 expression [].
In that study, high PD-L1 expression was associated with worse OS compared with low or negative PD-L1 expression (HR 2.61, 95% CI 1.31-5.22; P = 0.007).
Because only one eligible study was available, no quantitative meta-analysis was performed for OS/rwOS, and the result was summarized descriptively.
Nine studies were included in the main meta-analysis of PFS/rwPFS according to baseline ECOG performance status [, -, , , , ].
Effect direction was standardized as ECOG PS ≥ 2 versus ECOG PS 0-1 or < 2.
ECOG PS ≥ 2 was associated with a 74% higher hazard for the PFS/rwPFS endpoint (HR 1.74, 95% CI 1.36-2.22; P < 0.001; Fig. 5A).
Low-to-moderate heterogeneity was observed across the included studies (I2 = 30%; χ2 = 11.36, df = 8, P = 0.18).
A sensitivity analysis addressed potential cohort overlap within the ELUCIDATOR reports.

After replacing the ELUCIDATOR-derived estimate used in the main analysis with the corresponding alternative ELUCIDATOR estimate, the pooled association remained stable (HR 1.76, 95% CI 1.41-2.20; P < 0.001; I2 = 18%; Supplementary Fig. S6) [, ].
This result indicates that the association between ECOG PS ≥ 2 and shorter PFS/rwPFS was not materially affected by the selected ELUCIDATOR-derived estimate.
For OS/rwOS, five studies were included according to baseline ECOG performance status [, , , , ].
ECOG PS ≥ 2 was associated with more than a two-fold higher hazard of death compared with ECOG PS 0-1 or < 2 (HR 2.32, 95% CI 1.77-3.04; P < 0.001; Fig. 5B).
Moderate heterogeneity was observed across the included studies (I2 = 60%; χ2 = 9.94, df = 4, P = 0.04).
Sensitivity analyses examined the influence of cohort overlap and effect-estimate selection on the OS/rwOS result.

In the cohort-overlap analysis, the ELUCIDATOR-derived estimate used in the main analysis was replaced by the alternative ELUCIDATOR estimate because both estimates were derived from the ELUCIDATOR cohort.
The pooled estimate was nearly unchanged (HR 2.34, 95% CI 1.78-3.08; P < 0.001; I2 = 61%; Supplementary Fig. S7) [, ].
In an expanded-eligibility analysis, an additional extractable adjusted OS estimate was included, although the estimate was imprecise and directionally inconsistent with the main pooled effect [].
The pooled association remained significant after its inclusion (HR 2.25, 95% CI 1.72-2.95; P < 0.001; I2 = 56%; Supplementary Fig. S8).
These findings indicate that ECOG PS ≥ 2 was consistently associated with poorer OS/rwOS, although moderate between-study heterogeneity persisted in the OS/rwOS analysis.
Four studies were included in the main meta-analysis of PFS/rwPFS according to baseline CNS/brain metastasis status [, , , ].
Effect direction was standardized as CNS/brain metastasis present versus absent.
Baseline CNS/brain metastasis was associated with a 40% higher hazard for the PFS/rwPFS endpoint (HR 1.40, 95% CI 1.09-1.80; P = 0.008; Fig. 6A).
No statistical heterogeneity was observed across the included studies (I2 = 0%; χ2 = 2.29, df = 3, P = 0.51).
Sensitivity analyses evaluated whether the pooled PFS/rwPFS estimate was influenced by the definition of CNS involvement or by inclusion of unadjusted estimates.
In the non-standard definition analysis, an additional study was included because it reported CNS metastasis with unstable symptoms rather than ordinary CNS/brain metastasis [].
The pooled association remained significant (HR 1.53, 95% CI 1.12-2.09; P = 0.007; I2 = 30%; Supplementary Fig. S9).
In the expanded effect-estimate analysis, an extractable unadjusted HR for PFS was additionally included [].
The pooled result was also consistent with the main analysis (HR 1.44, 95% CI 1.13-1.83; P = 0.003; I2 = 0%; Supplementary Fig. S10).
These findings suggest that the association between baseline CNS/brain metastasis and shorter PFS/rwPFS was generally stable across alternative analytical assumptions.
Four studies were included in the meta-analysis of OS/rwOS according to baseline CNS/brain metastasis status [, , , ].
Baseline CNS/brain metastasis was associated with a 28% higher hazard of death compared with absence of CNS/brain metastasis (HR 1.28, 95% CI 1.10-1.48; P = 0.001; Fig. 6B).
No statistical heterogeneity was observed across the included studies (I2 = 0%; χ2 = 1.69, df = 3, P = 0.64).
No additional sensitivity analysis was performed for OS/rwOS because no corresponding alternative CNS/brain metastasis estimates were available for the predefined sensitivity scenarios.
Six studies were included in the main meta-analysis of PFS/rwPFS according to baseline liver metastasis status [, , , , , ].
Effect direction was standardized as liver metastasis present versus absent.
Baseline liver metastasis was associated with more than a two-fold higher hazard for the PFS/rwPFS endpoint (HR 2.25, 95% CI 1.54-3.28; P < 0.001; Fig. 7A).
Moderate heterogeneity was observed across the included studies (I2 = 53%; χ2 = 10.56, df = 5, P = 0.06).
A sensitivity analysis examined whether the pooled PFS/rwPFS estimate was influenced by inclusion of a small and directionally atypical estimate [].

After inclusion of this estimate, the association between liver metastasis and shorter PFS/rwPFS remained statistically significant (HR 2.15, 95% CI 1.49-3.11; P < 0.001; I2 = 49%; Supplementary Fig. S11).
This result indicates that the PFS/rwPFS finding was not materially altered by inclusion of the additional small-subgroup estimate.
For OS/rwOS, three studies were included according to baseline liver metastasis status [, , ].
Baseline liver metastasis was associated with a 56% higher hazard of death compared with absence of liver metastasis (HR 1.56, 95% CI 1.13-2.15; P = 0.007; Fig. 7B).
Substantial heterogeneity was observed across the included studies (I2 = 66%; χ2 = 5.97, df = 2, P = 0.05).
A sensitivity analysis assessed the influence of a directionally inconsistent and imprecise OS estimate [].
After this estimate was added, the pooled association was attenuated and no longer statistically significant (HR 1.41, 95% CI 0.95-2.10; P = 0.09; I2 = 72%; Supplementary Fig. S12).

Therefore, although the main OS/rwOS analysis suggested an adverse association between liver metastasis and survival, this result should be interpreted cautiously because it was sensitive to inclusion of the directionally inconsistent estimate and showed substantial between-study heterogeneity.
Five studies were included in the meta-analysis of PFS/rwPFS according to baseline bone metastasis status [, , , , ].
Effect direction was standardized as bone metastasis present versus absent.
Baseline bone metastasis was not significantly associated with PFS/rwPFS (HR 1.18, 95% CI 0.90-1.54; P = 0.23; Fig. 8A).
Moderate heterogeneity was observed across the included studies (I2 = 43%; χ2 = 6.99, df = 4, P = 0.14).
Three studies contributed to the main OS/rwOS analysis according to baseline bone metastasis status [, , ].
Baseline bone metastasis was associated with worse OS/rwOS in the main analysis (HR 1.39, 95% CI 1.08-1.79; P = 0.01; Fig. 8B).
Moderate heterogeneity was observed across the included studies (I2 = 42%; χ2 = 3.43, df = 2, P = 0.18).
A sensitivity analysis assessed the influence of a directionally inconsistent estimate [].
After this estimate was added, the pooled association was attenuated and no longer statistically significant (HR 1.15, 95% CI 0.72-1.84; P = 0.57; I2 = 79%; Supplementary Fig. S13).

Therefore, although the main OS/rwOS analysis suggested an adverse association between bone metastasis and survival, this finding should be interpreted cautiously because it was sensitive to inclusion of the directionally inconsistent estimate and showed substantial heterogeneity in the sensitivity analysis.
Formal assessment of publication bias was not performed because no individual meta-analysis included at least 10 studies.
The evidence-tier summary is presented in Table 3.

EGFR L858R, ECOG PS ≥ 2, and CNS/brain metastasis were classified as high-certainty adverse prognostic factors because they showed consistent adverse associations across endpoints or sensitivity analyses.

Liver metastasis was classified as moderate certainty for PFS/rwPFS but low certainty for OS/rwOS because the survival association was endpoint-dependent and sensitive to alternative estimate selection.

TP53 mutation, PD-L1 expression, and bone metastasis were classified as low-certainty or exploratory findings because of sparse evidence, instability in sensitivity analyses, or lack of a robust primary endpoint association.

This review synthesized available evidence on baseline clinical and molecular prognostic factors associated with poorer outcomes in patients with EGFR-mutated advanced NSCLC treated with first-line osimertinib.
The central finding is that risk after first-line osimertinib is not defined by one variable.
Instead, it appears to arise from three overlapping domains: tumor genotype, host functional reserve, and metastatic pattern.
EGFR L858R, compared with exon 19 deletion, showed the most consistent adverse association with both PFS/rwPFS and OS/rwOS.
TP53 mutation also showed adverse associations across endpoints, although fewer studies were available.
Among clinical factors, ECOG PS ≥ 2 and baseline CNS/brain metastasis were associated with inferior PFS/rwPFS and OS/rwOS.
Liver metastasis was strongly associated with shorter PFS/rwPFS, whereas its OS/rwOS association was less stable after inclusion of an alternative directionally inconsistent estimate.
Bone metastasis was not associated with PFS/rwPFS, and its apparent OS/rwOS association was unstable in sensitivity analysis.
High PD-L1 expression was associated with shorter PFS/rwPFS in the main analysis, but the finding was sensitive to alternative effect-estimate selection.
These results support risk stratification that combines molecular context, performance status, and metastatic distribution rather than relying on any single marker.

The strength of evidence differed across factors, with more consistent findings for EGFR L858R, ECOG PS ≥ 2, and CNS/brain metastasis than for TP53 mutation, PD-L1 expression, liver metastasis for OS/rwOS, or bone metastasis.
Among the molecular prognostic factors evaluated, EGFR L858R showed the most consistent adverse association with outcomes after first-line osimertinib.

Compared with exon 19 deletion, L858R was associated with shorter PFS/rwPFS in eight studies (HR 1.62, 95% CI 1.39-1.90) and worse OS/rwOS in seven studies (HR 1.63, 95% CI 1.40-1.88), with no detectable heterogeneity in either analysis.

This association also remained stable after replacement of one overlapping ELUCIDATOR-derived estimate with an alternative estimate from the same cohort [, ] and after inclusion of a lower-priority unadjusted PFS estimate [].

These findings are clinically relevant because exon 19 deletion and L858R are often grouped together as canonical sensitizing EGFR mutations in trial eligibility and routine practice, although their outcomes may not be equivalent.

Consistent with this observation, a nationwide Dutch registry study and a large US clinicogenomic cohort also reported less favorable survival among patients with L858R than among those with exon 19 deletion [, ].
A biological basis for this difference is plausible.

Structure-based analyses indicate that EGFR mutations differ in kinase conformation and drug sensitivity, and that structural classification may better predict EGFR-TKI response than exon-based grouping alone [].

Subgroup analyses from other EGFR-directed clinical programs have also shown that treatment effects may differ between exon 19 deletion and L858R, supporting the need for prespecified mutation-subtype stratification in future studies [].
The key clinical interpretation is not that L858R alone causes osimertinib resistance or mandates escalation.
Rather, L858R may shift the baseline risk distribution and should be incorporated as one component of integrated clinical-molecular risk assessment.
TP53 mutation was another adverse molecular feature, although the evidence base was narrower than that for EGFR L858R.
TP53 mutation was associated with shorter PFS/rwPFS in two studies (HR 1.65, 95% CI 1.15-2.37) and worse OS/rwOS in three studies (HR 1.55, 95% CI 1.14-2.12) [, , ].

This directionally consistent signal is supported by broader EGFR-TKI literature, including a prior meta-analysis that reported adverse associations between TP53 co-mutation and both PFS (HR 1.67) and OS (HR 1.89) [].
Mechanistically, TP53 mutation may reflect greater genomic instability, reduced oncogene dependence, and increased capacity for resistance evolution [].

However, TP53 status should not be treated as a uniform binary marker because its prognostic effect may vary by mutation type, functional domain, allelic state, clonality, and co-mutational background.
Concurrent RB1 and TP53 alterations have also been linked to lineage plasticity and histologic transformation in EGFR-mutant lung cancer [].

Therefore, the present meta-analysis pooled only comparable TP53 mutation-level estimates and did not treat p53 protein expression or composite co-alteration patterns as interchangeable surrogates for TP53 mutation status [, , ].

Overall, TP53 mutation appears clinically relevant, but the evidence remains less extensive than that for EGFR L858R, and its use in risk stratification requires standardized reporting of mutation class, sequencing platform, allelic context, and co-mutational background.
Among exploratory molecular markers, PD-L1 expression showed a less stable prognostic signal than EGFR L858R or TP53 mutation.
In the main PFS/rwPFS analysis, high PD-L1 expression was associated with shorter PFS/rwPFS (HR 1.84, 95% CI 1.15-2.95) [, ].
This association remained significant when a study using a lower TPS cutoff of ≥ 20% was added [], but became non-significant after inclusion of a directionally inconsistent estimate [].
For OS/rwOS, only one eligible study was available, and quantitative synthesis was not possible [].

Therefore, current evidence suggests that high PD-L1 expression may be associated with less favorable outcomes in some first-line osimertinib-treated cohorts, but this finding remains unstable, low-certainty, and hypothesis-generating.
Accordingly, PD-L1 expression should be regarded as an exploratory prognostic signal rather than a clinically actionable biomarker in the first-line osimertinib setting.

This interpretation is consistent with the broader context of EGFR-mutated NSCLC, in which PD-L1 expression does not have the same predictive meaning as in unselected NSCLC treated with immune checkpoint inhibitors; for example, a phase II trial of pembrolizumab in EGFR-mutant, PD-L1-positive, TKI-naive advanced NSCLC was stopped early for futility [].

Other emerging molecular markers also remain exploratory rather than definitive in the first-line osimertinib setting. ctDNA-based variables, including baseline plasma detectability, EGFR mutation abundance, adjusted variant allele frequency, and molecular clearance, may capture systemic tumor burden, tumor shedding, spatial heterogeneity, and early molecular persistence [, , , ].
However, definitions, assay platforms, sampling time points, and cutoffs varied substantially, preventing firm quantitative synthesis.

Similar caution applies to NRG1 alterations, AXL expression, p53 protein expression, and uncommon co-alteration patterns, which were generally evaluated in single cohorts and did not provide comparable HRs across both PFS/rwPFS and OS/rwOS [, ].

Future studies should evaluate these exploratory markers within integrated models that combine tissue next-generation sequencing, plasma ctDNA features, EGFR mutation subtype, co-mutation profile, metastatic pattern, and host clinical status, with standardized assays and prospective validation.
Among clinical factors, ECOG PS ≥ 2 was one of the most consistent and readily available prognostic factors associated with poorer outcome.
Patients with ECOG PS ≥ 2 had shorter PFS/rwPFS (HR 1.74, 95% CI 1.36-2.22) and worse OS/rwOS (HR 2.32, 95% CI 1.77-3.04).

The PFS/rwPFS finding showed only low-to-moderate heterogeneity, and the OS/rwOS association remained stable after alternative handling of overlapping ELUCIDATOR-derived estimates and after inclusion of an additional adjusted OS estimate [21,27,28].
ECOG PS ≥ 2 should be interpreted as a composite marker reflecting functional decline, comorbidity, frailty, nutritional compromise, treatment continuity, and access to subsequent therapy.
Real-world first-line osimertinib data support this interpretation because FLAURA-ineligible patients had shorter survival, and ECOG PS ≥ 2 was a major reason for trial ineligibility [].
However, poor PS should refine risk assessment rather than exclude patients from osimertinib.

Prospective and retrospective poor-PS studies reported clinically meaningful response and PS improvement with first-line osimertinib, although outcomes were poorer in patients with PS 3-4 than in those with PS 2 [-].
Therefore, ECOG PS ≥ 2 should prompt closer early reassessment, symptom control, supportive-care integration, toxicity surveillance, and treatment-continuity planning.
Baseline CNS/brain metastasis was another clinically meaningful prognostic factor, but its interpretation requires caution because osimertinib has established intracranial activity.

In the present analysis, baseline CNS/brain metastasis was associated with shorter PFS/rwPFS (HR 1.40, 95% CI 1.09-1.80) and worse OS/rwOS (HR 1.28, 95% CI 1.10-1.48), with no detectable heterogeneity in either main analysis [, , , , , ].
The PFS/rwPFS association also remained significant after inclusion of a non-standardly defined symptomatic CNS cohort [] and an additional unadjusted PFS estimate [].
These findings should not be interpreted as evidence that osimertinib is ineffective in the CNS.
In FLAURA, osimertinib reduced the risk of CNS progression or death compared with first-generation EGFR-TKIs among patients with baseline CNS metastases [].

Osimertinib also showed activity in more difficult intracranial disease; in BLOOM, patients with EGFR-mutated NSCLC and leptomeningeal metastases achieved a leptomeningeal ORR of 62%, median PFS of 8.6 months, and median OS of 11.0 months [].
Therefore, the adverse association observed in this meta-analysis is better understood as a marker of disease phenotype than as a lack of CNS efficacy.
Baseline CNS involvement may reflect earlier metastatic dissemination, neurotropic disease behavior, and more complex intracranial-extracranial disease dynamics.
Clinically, it should identify patients who require structured intracranial surveillance and multidisciplinary assessment.

Brain metastasis management should still consider lesion number, lesion size, symptoms, edema, neurologic risk, prior local therapy, extracranial disease status, and patient preference, consistent with EANO-ESMO guidance emphasizing individualized treatment and follow-up [].

Thus, baseline CNS/brain metastasis should be used as a risk-stratification and monitoring variable, but it should not by itself mandate upfront local therapy or first-line treatment escalation without prospective validation.
Liver metastasis showed a strong association with shorter PFS/rwPFS, whereas its OS/rwOS association was less stable.

In the present analysis, baseline liver metastasis was associated with substantially shorter PFS/rwPFS (HR 2.25, 95% CI 1.54-3.28), and this association remained significant after inclusion of a small and directionally atypical estimate [].
By contrast, the OS/rwOS association was attenuated and became non-significant after inclusion of an imprecise and directionally inconsistent estimate [].
This endpoint-specific pattern is clinically plausible.

PFS/rwPFS is closer to first-line disease control, whereas OS/rwOS is shaped by post-progression survival, subsequent therapy, competing risks, baseline liver function, extrahepatic disease burden, and cohort composition.
Differences in imaging frequency or progression ascertainment may also influence apparent time to progression, but this could not be evaluated from aggregate data.
External EGFR-mutant NSCLC data support the adverse direction.
In a multicenter study of patients receiving first-line EGFR-TKIs, liver metastasis was associated with shorter PFS (7.5 vs. 11.8 months) and shorter OS (20.8 vs. 30.6 months) [].

More recent EGFR-mutant data also suggest that liver metastasis may correlate with higher tumor abundance and poorer outcomes, supporting the view that hepatic involvement reflects systemic disease burden rather than a purely anatomical feature [].
Therefore, liver metastasis should be retained as an important high-risk baseline feature, particularly for PFS/rwPFS.
Its OS/rwOS effect should be interpreted more cautiously.

Baseline bone metastasis was not associated with the primary PFS/rwPFS endpoint (HR 1.18, 95% CI 0.90-1.54), and its apparent OS/rwOS association became non-significant after inclusion of a directionally inconsistent estimate [].
Therefore, available study-level data do not confirm bone metastasis as a robust prognostic factor for first-line osimertinib outcomes.
This does not mean that skeletal disease is clinically unimportant; rather, a binary present-versus-absent variable is probably too crude.
Bone metastasis spans a broad spectrum of lesion number, distribution, morphology, pain burden, fracture risk, spinal cord compression risk, local radiotherapy, and exposure to bone-targeted agents.

In one multicenter cohort of 250 patients with EGFR-mutated NSCLC treated with osimertinib, 51% had bone metastases at osimertinib initiation, 39% of those with bone metastases experienced at least one skeletal-related event, and only 16% received bone-targeted agents [].
Osteoblastic bone reaction may further complicate radiologic assessment and should not be mistaken for progression [].
Future prognostic studies should incorporate skeletal disease burden, symptoms, skeletal-related events, lesion morphology, local treatment, and bone-modifying therapy exposure.
The clinical relevance of these findings is increasing as the first-line treatment landscape for EGFR-mutated advanced NSCLC moves beyond osimertinib monotherapy.
FLAURA2 and MARIPOSA have shown that intensified first-line strategies can improve outcomes compared with osimertinib alone in selected contexts [-].
The final OS analysis of MARIPOSA further supported an OS advantage for amivantamab-lazertinib, but this benefit was accompanied by a higher incidence of grade 3 or higher adverse events [].
A secondary MARIPOSA analysis also explored outcomes in patients with biomarkers or clinical features considered high risk [].

However, the present meta-analysis did not include osimertinib-based combination-therapy cohorts contributing comparable prognostic HRs and therefore cannot inform selection between osimertinib monotherapy and intensified first-line regimens.
The clinically useful output of the present meta-analysis is not a treatment-selection rule, but an evidence map for baseline prognostic risk assessment.

For example, from a prognostic-risk perspective, a patient with EGFR L858R, TP53 mutation, ECOG PS ≥ 2, and liver or CNS involvement differs clinically from a patient with isolated exon 19 deletion, good performance status, and limited extracranial disease, even if both receive the same first-line EGFR-TKI.

Future studies should test integrated clinical-molecular risk models and determine prospectively whether patients with adverse prognostic profiles derive differential benefit from intensified first-line strategies, closer surveillance, broader molecular profiling, or early supportive-care intervention.
Interpretation of these findings depends on the separation between main and sensitivity analyses.

In prognostic-factor meta-analyses, pooling every extractable HR without regard to cohort overlap, adjustment strategy, exposure definition, endpoint ascertainment, and reporting quality can create misleading certainty [].
Therefore, the main analyses prioritized non-overlapping cohorts, standard exposure definitions, directly reported estimates, and adjusted HRs when available.
Estimates affected by overlap, non-standard definitions, unadjusted modeling, small exposed subgroups, or directionally inconsistent results were examined in sensitivity analyses.

Where data permitted, restricted sensitivity analyses were used to examine whether key associations were disproportionately influenced by study design or by ELUCIDATOR-derived estimates; however, many factor-outcome pairs remained too sparsely populated for reliable design-stratified pooling.

This approach helped identify an evidence hierarchy: EGFR L858R, ECOG PS ≥ 2, and CNS/brain metastasis remained stable across key sensitivity analyses, and liver metastasis showed a robust PFS/rwPFS association [, , -].
By contrast, PD-L1 expression, liver metastasis for OS/rwOS, and bone metastasis for OS/rwOS were sensitive to alternative estimate selection and should remain hypothesis-generating [, ].
In line with GRADE guidance for prognostic factors, inconsistency, imprecision, indirectness, and risk of bias should lower confidence in specific prognostic associations [].
Statistical significance in a main model alone should therefore not be equated with robust prognostic evidence.
This review has several strengths.
The protocol was prospectively registered, and the review question, eligibility criteria, outcome hierarchy, and synthesis plan were defined before pooling.
The search strategy was designed to capture first-line osimertinib prognostic studies even when individual factors were reported only in tables, figures, or supplementary materials.

The analysis considered both molecular and clinical prognostic factors, standardized effect directions, prioritized adjusted estimates when available, handled overlapping cohorts conservatively, and used sensitivity analyses to distinguish stable associations from exploratory signals.
These steps improved transparency and allow readers to trace how each prognostic factor contributed to the overall evidence pattern.
Several limitations should be acknowledged.
Most included studies were observational or real-world cohorts, so residual confounding cannot be excluded despite adjustment in individual studies.

Because this review was based on aggregate study-level data rather than individual patient data, uniform confounder adjustment, consistent subgroup definitions, and formal assessment of interactions between prognostic factors were not possible.

Although covariates included in adjusted models were extracted and summarized, differences in multivariable adjustment across studies remained an additional source of methodological heterogeneity that could not be fully captured by the I2 statistic.

Definitions and measurement methods also varied across studies, particularly for rwPFS, PD-L1 cutoffs, CNS involvement, ctDNA-based biomarkers, metastatic-site reporting, and progression ascertainment.
Combining trial-defined and real-world endpoints may therefore have introduced endpoint heterogeneity.

In addition, the assembled evidence base contained no osimertinib-based combination-therapy cohorts with comparable prognostic HRs; consequently, the planned monotherapy-versus-combination subgroup analysis could not be performed, and the aggregate data could not assess treatment-by-biomarker interactions or differential benefit from treatment intensification.
Several pooled analyses included few studies, limiting publication-bias assessment and restricting the feasibility of study-design or data-source sensitivity analyses.
NOS and RoB 2 were used according to study design and were not interpreted as directly comparable numeric quality scales.
Findings for TP53 mutation, PD-L1 expression, liver metastasis for OS/rwOS, and bone metastasis should therefore be interpreted cautiously.

Several potentially relevant prognostic factors, including MET amplification, EGFR mutation abundance, ctDNA positivity, NRG1 alterations, AXL expression, p53 expression, metastatic burden, and response outcomes, could not be pooled because comparable effect estimates were limited or definitions were inconsistent.
Finally, although overlapping cohorts were handled conservatively, complete independence across all reports could not always be verified.

Geographic or ethnic generalizability may also be limited because a substantial proportion of included studies were Japanese or other Asian cohorts, and several pooled estimates included ELUCIDATOR-derived reports.

Differences in EGFR-mutant NSCLC epidemiology, TKI exposure, imaging and follow-up practice, subsequent treatment access, and real-world data capture may affect extrapolation to non-Asian populations.
Restriction to English-language full-text studies may also have introduced language or publication bias.

In patients with EGFR-mutated advanced NSCLC treated with first-line osimertinib, evidence-tier assessment identified EGFR L858R, ECOG PS ≥ 2, and baseline CNS/brain metastasis as high-certainty adverse prognostic factors.
Liver metastasis showed moderate-certainty evidence for PFS/rwPFS but lower-certainty evidence for OS/rwOS.

TP53 mutation, PD-L1 expression, and bone metastasis should be interpreted as lower-certainty or exploratory findings because of sparse evidence, endpoint dependence, or sensitivity-analysis instability.

These findings should be interpreted as prognostic associations within a common first-line osimertinib treatment background, not as predictive biomarkers or stand-alone evidence for treatment intensification.
Prospective studies and individual patient data analyses are needed to develop and validate integrated risk-stratification models.
